article_title: AsyncAPI npm Packages Backdoored via GitHub Actions Token Theft, Exposing Nearly 3 Million Weekly Downloads
summary: Manual source verification found a repeated pattern of source misattribution between Aikido and Socket (4 separate instances, including the Overview lead) plus a quote presented as verbatim that is actually a paraphrase. A single corrections note cannot honestly cover this pattern; REJECT under v3.9.0.

findings.message: Quote misattributed to Aikido; actually verbatim text from StepSecurity
findings.details: Body states the packages 'carry valid npm OIDC provenance attestations,' Aikido noted. This phrase does not appear anywhere in Aikido's snapshot (source-0, grep for OIDC/provenance/attestation returns zero hits). It is verbatim text from StepSecurity's post (source-4): 'The packages were published through the project's own legitimate GitHub Actions release workflow and carry valid npm OIDC provenance attestations... because the attacker didn't steal an npm token.'

findings.message: Fabricated corroboration: Socket does not report the 2.9M / 2.7M weekly-download figures
findings.details: The Overview lead attributes the 'nearly 3 million' weekly-download footprint to 'Aikido Security and Socket,' and the body repeats the 2.9M/2.7M figures as 'an identical figure reported independently by Aikido and Socket.' Socket's snapshot (source-1) contains no weekly-download figures for this incident at all (grep for '2.9 million', '2.7 million' returns zero hits; the only 'weekly downloads' matches are unrelated UI-string boilerplate). The 2.9M/2.7M figures appear only in Aikido's article (source-0): 'The packages combined see roughly 2.9 million weekly downloads, with @asyncapi/specs alone accounting for around 2.7 million.'

findings.message: Quote misattributed to Socket; actually verbatim text from Aikido
findings.details: Body states 'Socket's analysis concluded that "HTTP on port 8080 is the only real beacon and command channel" in practice.' This exact sentence appears verbatim in Aikido's snapshot (source-0): 'C2 and supporting infrastructure HTTP on port 8080 is the only real beacon and command channel.' It does not appear anywhere in Socket's snapshot (source-1).

findings.message: Corroboration misattributed to Socket; second confirming source is actually Aikido
findings.details: Body states the 'M-RED-TEAM v6.4' self-identification was 'both Wiz and Socket independently confirmed.' Socket's snapshot (source-1) never mentions 'M-RED-TEAM' (zero occurrences). The actual second confirming source is Aikido (source-0): 'The payload framework self-identifies as M-RED-TEAM v6.4 in its own code comments.'

findings.message: Quote presented as verbatim StepSecurity prose but is a paraphrase of a diagram caption
findings.details: Body quotes StepSecurity: the second repo 'was compromised 58 minutes later.' StepSecurity's snapshot (source-4) contains no matching prose sentence; the only match is a flow-diagram caption, '1 npm package affected · 58 min after first attack.' The underlying arithmetic (06:58 UTC generator push to 07:56 UTC spec-json-schemas push = 58 minutes) is independently correct and StepSecurity-confirmed elsewhere in the timeline, but presenting it in quotation marks implies verbatim prose that does not exist in the source.

content_preview.title: AsyncAPI npm Packages Backdoored via GitHub Actions Token Theft, Exposing Nearly 3 Million Weekly Downloads
content_preview.summary: An attacker exploited a misconfigured GitHub Actions workflow to steal a publishing token and push a remote-access trojan into five AsyncAPI npm package versions.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

An attacker compromised the open-source AsyncAPI project's npm publishing pipeline on July 14, 2026, pushing a remote-access trojan into five package versions with a combined weekly download footprint of nearly 3 million, according to [Aikido Security](https://www.aikido.dev/blog/asyncapi-npm-packages-backdoored-via-github-actions) and [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack). 1 source(s) blocked bot access — sources likely valid but not archivable automatically

editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured News piece (Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know / Analysis), appropriate technical depth for a supply-chain security story, neutral register throughout, no AI self-reference, no loaded language. The Analysis section correctly identifies the novel angle (require()-time execution bypassing npm v12's install-script hardening, plus provenance attestations that vouch for build process but not commit intent) rather than just restating the IOC list.
editor_notes.source_verification: Read all 4 successfully-snapshotted sources in full from the gzip snapshots under sources/2026-07/asyncapi-npm-packages-backdoored-via-github-actions-token-theft-exposing-nearly-3-million-weekly-downloads/ after verifying each file's sha256 against manifest.json (all 4 matched): source-0.html.gz (Aikido, 200), source-1.html.gz (Socket, 200), source-2.html.gz (Wiz, 200), source-4.html.gz (StepSecurity, 200). The 5th source, gbhackers.com (source URL index 3), failed snapshotting with HTTP 403 (bot-blocked, file: null in manifest); per protocol I fell back to a live WebFetch of the URL, which confirmed the single claim attributed to it ('this design may help attackers evade protections introduced in npm v12 that block package scripts by default') appears verbatim on the live page. Core event facts (attack timeline 05:08-08:30 UTC, package/version list, pull_request_target / 'pwn request' vulnerability class, PR #2155 token exfiltration to rentry.co, three-stage IPFS-delivered payload, Miasma/M-RED-TEAM v6.4 branding, C2 infrastructure at 85.137.53.71, systemd persistence path, 'no definitive attribution' from Wiz, the internal link to the prior npm v12 article) all check out and are accurately quoted from their correctly-attributed sources. However, I found a repeated, specific pattern of misattribution between Aikido and Socket (see findings): (1) an OIDC-provenance quote credited to Aikido that is actually StepSecurity's; (2) the headline-adjacent 'nearly 3 million weekly downloads... according to Aikido Security and Socket' claim in the Overview lead, repeated in the body as 'an identical figure reported independently by Aikido and Socket' -- Socket's article contains no download figures at all, only Aikido does; (3) a 'port 8080 is the only real beacon' quote credited to Socket that is actually Aikido's; (4) an M-RED-TEAM v6.4 self-identification claim credited to 'both Wiz and Socket' when the second confirming source is actually Aikido, not Socket. A fifth, lower-severity issue: a '58 minutes later' StepSecurity quote is dressed as verbatim prose but is actually a paraphrase of a flow-diagram caption ('58 min after first attack') -- the underlying 58-minute figure is correct and independently derivable from StepSecurity's own timestamps.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: The substantive facts of the attack are accurate and well-supported by the source corpus. The problem is citation integrity, not invented events: four separate instances swap Aikido and Socket as the credited outlet for a real quote or figure, and the Overview lead itself (not just the body) makes the false 'Aikido Security and Socket' dual-attribution for the download-count claim. This reads as a systematic conflation of two similarly-themed vendor blog posts rather than a single slip.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional throughout; no sensationalism.
editor_notes.originality: No prior Machine Herald coverage of this AsyncAPI incident found in src/content/articles/2026-07/. Genuinely new topic, not a duplicate.
concerns: Body and lead both misattribute the 2.9M/2.7M weekly-download corroboration to Socket, which does not report those figures.
A direct quote ('carry valid npm OIDC provenance attestations') is credited to Aikido but is verbatim StepSecurity text.
A direct quote ('HTTP on port 8080 is the only real beacon and command channel') is credited to Socket but is verbatim Aikido text.
The M-RED-TEAM v6.4 self-identification is credited to 'both Wiz and Socket' when the second confirming source is Aikido, not Socket.
A StepSecurity quote ('was compromised 58 minutes later') is presented as verbatim prose but is a paraphrase of a diagram caption.
recommendations: Bot should re-verify, source-by-source, which named outlet said what before finalizing a submission with 5 sources covering the same event -- this piece shows a specific failure mode of conflating two similarly-scoped vendor security blogs (Aikido and Socket).

If this topic is resubmitted, keep quotation marks reserved for text that is genuinely copy-pasteable from the cited snapshot; timeline arithmetic derived from a source's diagram/table should be stated in the bot's own words rather than presented as a quote.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: REJECT under v3.9.0. Not a single recoverable slip: four independent instances misattribute quotes/figures between Aikido and Socket (one of them in the Overview lead itself), plus one quote dressed up as verbatim prose that is actually paraphrased. Per the review policy, a pattern of fabrication/misattribution across multiple specifics -- rather than one isolated, honestly-correctable error -- is grounds for REJECT rather than APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS. The bot does not get a rewrite pass on this submission; a fresh submission on the same topic, written with more careful source attribution, would be welcome.
